trailer.caption: Sovkora, the trailer: AI that stays home
trailer.alt: The Sovkora trailer, 1 min 51, music and no voice: Montréal at night, then seven generated characters who each run a Studio on their own machine, the ten packs, the engine and the editions. Its words are in the text version.

transcript.lead: Its words, as the film shows them (titles in French, subtitles in English):
lines: Every day, your data leaves.
What if it stayed?
Sovkora: AI that stays home.
Three things, done on your side.
01. Studios with a known price up front: a sentence or a file becomes an image, a video or a verified document. The estimated cost shows before you run it.
02. Every result keeps its run: the output, its steps, its input and its run id stay together. Any result can be checked again.
03. A chat and agents that ask first: the models run on your machines. An agent shows its plan and acts only once approved.
Éric asks a question. The answer is written on this machine.
Éric asks a question (chat, local models): the answer is written on this machine. The models run at his place; a hosted model only if he plugs one in.
Maya, real-estate agent (Real-Estate Reels): five photos become a Reel ready to publish. The estimated cost shows before she runs it.
Nadia, property manager (Document Verification): a lease against the rules of its jurisdiction, a PDF against tampering. Every finding cites its rule and the passage.
Théo, founder, sales (Outbound Prospecting): a list becomes a prioritised dossier, then a sequence. The agent shows its plan and waits for his yes.
Sam, data analyst (Data-driven UI): a CSV and a question become a live dashboard, on her own data.
Jules, video creator (Video analysis): what the video says, its keyframes, then three titles and tags to approve.
Léa, trust and safety (Media safety): photo, video or voice message, safe to show? An answer nobody could read is never a pass.

Ten packs, thirty-three Studios, one trade each: Real-Estate Studio, Media Studios, Outbound Prospecting, Recommendations & insights, Wellbeing, Document Verification, Media safety, Message authenticity, Profile photo check, Trade Showcase.

Wellbeing: put into words what you live through. Not care. Message authenticity: written by a person? A signal, never a verdict. Profile photo check: are these photos one real adult's profile? Trade Showcase: your job sites become a showcase that sells.
One engine. Clients, engine, workers and models: one request, five steps, one run record.
On your Mac. Your servers. Your phone.
37 models, 28 on your machines. 128 measured runs, 9 measured models, 0 telemetry calls.
Zero telemetry: nothing leaves. Price before, run id after.
Open source, Apache-2.0. The code is open. Read it. Run it. The engine, the pack interface, the command line and the reference packs are public.
A film made with Sovkora: 7 shots, $1.76 of GPU.
Community: open source, now. Business: soon. Entreprise: with Krizaka.
Sovkora, AI that stays home. sovkora.com. A Krizaka product, Montréal.

dossier-nadia.caption: Sovkora Files no. 01, Nadia: the lease that never left her office
dossier-nadia.alt: A fictional story, faces generated: Nadia, who manages 300 homes in Old Montréal, says no to every request to send her tenants' documents out. One evening a PDF looks too perfect; Sovkora's Document Verification Studio examines the file itself, and Nadia, not the machine, is the judge. 1 min 25, with sound; titles in French, with English subtitles.

transcript.lead: Its titles, as the film shows them (in French, with English subtitles):
lines: Old Montréal, 5:42 pm.
1,205 times, Nadia said no.
Can you email me the PDFs? No. Just a photo of the lease, then? No.
To everything that wanted her documents: no.
300 homes. 1,400 pages a month. Every page carries someone's name: a tenant, a supplier, an employee. Her documents don't leave her office. Period.
She reads everything. Leases, invoices, service contracts. But her eyes can't see who produced a PDF, or when, or whether it was touched up afterwards.
Nadia's rule: sending a lease « to the cloud » means taking it outside her walls. Nadia doesn't. Even when it's convenient. Especially when it's convenient.
Who produced it? When? The file is read here. It is sent nowhere.
Yes. Nadia said yes. Because this time, the document didn't move.

Document Verification, the file: the Studio examines the file itself, who produced it, when, with what, and whether it was edited afterwards, and lists the points worth clearing up. It never judges what the document says.
Why the 15th? Nadia is the judge. Not the machine.

The contract. Residential lease, Québec, 10 rules as they stood on 2024-02-21. Each finding gives its rule, its source and the passage of the document. The rules as they stood on a date you pick, not today's.
Classed sensitive: erased after 30 days, an append-only log, never used for training, out of scope: refused. Four controls applied by the engine. The pack can't opt out.
Should I get a lawyer? I draft and proofread documents. I don't give legal advice; for that, see a legal professional.
Reports. Never advice.
Nadia still says no. To everything else.
Sovkora, AI that stays home. sovkora.com. A Krizaka product, Montréal.

dossier-sam.caption: Sovkora Files no. 02, Sam: one CSV, one question, one dashboard
dossier-sam.alt: A fictional story, faces generated: Sam, an analyst in a Montréal office, rebuilds a dashboard by hand every night because her 4 GB file holds real customers' names and cannot leave. One question put to the CSV gives a dashboard where every number points to its row and column, and she goes home at 6:02 pm. 1 min 11, with sound; titles in French, with English subtitles.

transcript.lead: Its titles, as the film shows them (in French, with English subtitles):
lines: Montréal, 11:58 pm.
Sam lied. 110 times.
Is it ready? Almost. Every « almost » was a night.
The CSV was 4 GB. And it couldn't go anywhere: customers inside. Real ones. Names, addresses, amounts.
So Sam did what everyone does: she rebuilt the dashboard by hand. Until midnight. Then a bit later.
One CSV. One question. One dashboard. Every number comes from her data. And her data never left the room.
Why this number? Every number has a row and a column. Every answer keeps its run: output, steps, input, id. No black box.
Ask your question. (It became her favourite line.)
Sam went home at 6:02 pm. The CSV never left.
AI that stays home. Next file: Théo.

dossier-theo.caption: Sovkora Files no. 03, Théo: the machine shows, he decides
dossier-theo.alt: A fictional story, faces generated: Théo, a founder, pins forty-seven cards and twelve metres of red string to a wall and is sure the answer is Plateau. Sam exports the quarter's bookings, 1,840 a month across three studios, and asks one question; the machine shows the numbers, Théo decides, and nothing leaves the room. 1 min 15, with sound; titles in French, with English subtitles.

transcript.lead: Its titles, as the film shows them (in French, with English subtitles):
lines: Théo has a strategy. 10 metres of red string.
Plateau. It's obvious. Look at the wall.
The wall said: Plateau. Forty-seven cards, twelve metres of string and one conviction. The wall had never seen an invoice.
Sam exported the quarter. One file. One question. Ask your question.
1,840 bookings a month. Three studios. One question. Folioviv kept them. Sovkora read them. At their place: nothing left the room.
And where do those clients come from? 38% from Griffintown.
The machine shows. Théo decides.
You can take the string off now.
Sovkora, AI that stays home. Next file: Jules.

intro.title: A small Montréal studio. It builds in the open, with agents.
intro.lead: Krizaka is a small studio founded in Montréal. We build our software with AI agents, in the open, and we measure how we work. First Sovkora, the AI engine that stays with you. Then the products that run on it, Verikora first.

who.title: It started in Montréal
who.lead: Krizaka is a company founded in Montréal, a small studio. It builds its software with AI agents it directs and reviews, and it shows its work: the code, the tickets and the path of every change.
who.refusal: We started from one question: where was my document read, by which model, and who can see the result? Software that cannot answer asks for trust on faith. So what we ship is tested and documented, and the blocks it stands on are public.
creditsList: Titles set in code, in the faces of @krizaka/fonts
No voice, so no captions: the film's page describes each shot

name.title: A name that sounds like two memories
passage: Krizaka is not a dictionary word. To the founders, it first sounds like The King of Fighters and the arcade halls of their youth: the coin slipped into the slot, the close rounds, the rematch asked for right away.

It also sounds like korassa, كراسة, the Arabic word for a notebook. The school kind, filled in blue ink with a margin left for the corrections. That notebook became our identity: the paper, the blue ink, the margin.
Two memories, one name: play seriously, and write everything down.

card.caption: The name, and the word you hear in it.

work.title: A studio that works with agents
work.lead: Our software is written by AI agents, one lane per product, from a single board. Nothing merges by hand: a train carries every change to the main branch once its checks are green.

board.name: The board
board.line: Every piece of work starts from a ticket that says what will prove it done.

lane.name: One lane per product
lane.line: One agent session at a time per lane, on one ticket.

pr.name: The pull request
pr.line: The test first, then the code, in the open on GitHub.

train.name: The train
train.line: It merges when its turn comes, never by hand.

matrix.name: The matrix
matrix.line: A deterministic check, no AI: the reference of our rules, repository by repository.

depth: When a repository gets stuck on a red change, the crack is called. It starts from the goal: does each open change still make sense? It closes, folds or parks, and only then does it fix. It replaced the firefighter, who fixed first.

We measure our speed. In early November it dropped: gates added one by one were piling up. We kept what protects, such as security, secrets, accessibility and honest pages, and relaxed or removed what slowed us without protecting.
Every rule now says what it must improve, and it counts what it refuses. The first measure of this new way of working is set for November 8, 2026.

The person in charge of the protection of personal information is the president of the company; their title and contact are published in the next section.

sections.title: Privacy officer
paragraphs: Under Québec’s Law 25, the person in charge of the protection of personal information is published here.
Person in charge of the protection of personal information: the president of Technologies Krizaka Inc. — confidentialite@krizaka.com
Write to this address to access, correct or delete your information, withdraw a consent or file a complaint; we answer within 30 days.

sections.title: Our commitment
paragraphs: Krizaka builds software that keeps data where it belongs. This page says what this website collects, what it does with it and who handles it. If a practice is not written here, it does not happen.

sections.title: What this website collects
paragraphs: The only way you give us personal information is the contact form. We receive your name, your e-mail address, your organisation if you give it, the topic, the timing if you give it, your message, the language of the page and the page you came from (so we know which product you asked about).

Before the message reaches us, two checks protect the form: Cloudflare Turnstile checks that a person sends it (it receives your IP address for that), and a six-digit code, valid for 15 minutes, is sent to your e-mail address; the message leaves only once you enter that code.

We use them only to reply to you. By sending the form you agree that we use them for that. We do not sell them, share them for marketing, use them to profile you or send you anything you did not ask for.

The message is delivered to the team by e-mail, through our e-mail provider Mailgun, and may also be posted to a private team messaging channel. We keep it as long as the conversation needs it, then delete it.
To limit abuse, the server counts messages per IP address in memory (five every ten minutes). That count is not written anywhere and disappears when the server restarts.

sections.title: Technical data
paragraphs: Like any web host, the platform that serves this website keeps technical logs — IP address, time, page requested, browser — for security and abuse prevention, under its own policy.

Images, videos and recordings are served from a content delivery network (Bunny). Your browser contacts it directly when a page loads them, so it sees your IP address and the request, as any server does. Fonts and scripts are served by krizaka.com itself.

This website measures no audience today: no analytics tool, no advertising, no tracking pixel and no social-network widget. If it ever counts its visits, our own server will do it, without a cookie, an identifier or a stored IP address and without a third-party tool, and this page will say so first.

sections.title: Cookies and local storage
paragraphs: One functional cookie, NEXT_LOCALE, remembers the language you chose (one year). Your theme preference (dark or light) is kept in your browser's local storage, under the name kz-theme.
No analytics cookie, no advertising cookie, no third-party cookie. Because both items only remember a choice you made, no consent banner is shown.

sections.title: Krizaka accounts (blog.krizaka.com)
paragraphs: Not open yet: the blog's sign-in is switched on only once this service runs, and until then none of the data below is collected. This section says now what will happen then.

The blog lets you sign in with GitHub, Google, Apple or Facebook to comment, receive replies and keep your saved posts on every device. Signing in creates a Krizaka account, held by accounts.krizaka.com. It is not an account of any of our products: Sovkora, Verikora and the others keep their own users, and a Krizaka account gives no access to them.

We keep the provider you used and its identifier for you, the e-mail address that provider verified, your display name, your comments, the posts you saved, and whether you want reply e-mails. We use them only to run your account: show your name next to your comments, keep your saved posts, and — only if you turn it on — tell you by e-mail that someone replied. No password, no IP address kept, no profiling, no advertising.

Your first comment waits for a moderator before it appears; comments can be reported and hidden pending review. Comments are checked by Cloudflare Turnstile against abuse. Reply e-mails go through our e-mail provider, Mailgun, and each one has a one-click unsubscribe link.

The data is stored in Krizaka's database on DigitalOcean (Toronto). From your account page you can download everything your account holds as a file, remove a sign-in provider, stop reply e-mails, or delete the account: the account, its saved posts and settings are deleted, and its comments too (a deleted comment that has replies keeps its place without text or name). Posts saved without an account stay in your browser only.

sections.title: Our software
paragraphs: The building blocks (Krizaka UI, Krizaka Java, Krizaka TypeScript) are open source: they run on your infrastructure and process data under your control. They send us no telemetry. Sovkora, Verikora and Folioviv are in development, their sign-up is closed and they collect nothing through this site; Kridoc is in design.
If you connect external services to them (AI providers, payment gateways, video CDN), the data you send goes directly to those providers under their own policies.

sections.title: Who handles data for us
paragraphs: DigitalOcean — hosts this website and the development environment (Toronto, Canada).
Bunny.net — serves media (images, videos, recordings) of this website, and videos of the development environment.
Mailgun — delivers the contact-form e-mails and those of the development environment.
Cloudflare — checks, with Turnstile, that a person sends the contact form.
GitHub and npm — host our code and packages. They are not involved when you read this site; they receive the data you give them if you follow a link and use them, under their own policies.
Where this data is, and the assessment the law requires before it leaves Québec, are in the next section. The list is complete as of the date above.

sections.title: Outside Québec: where your information goes
paragraphs: Under section 17 of Québec's Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, a business must assess the privacy factors before it communicates personal information outside Québec: how sensitive it is, what it will be used for, what protects it, contracts included, and the legal framework of the place it goes to. The communication must also be covered by a written agreement.

Today, what you give us through this website leaves Québec. This website's server is at DigitalOcean, in Toronto, Ontario: in Canada, but outside Québec. The contact form's e-mails go through Mailgun, in the United States. The bot check goes through Cloudflare, which receives your IP address. Media are served by Bunny, a content delivery network whose servers are spread around the world; we are preparing their move to DigitalOcean, in Toronto.
That assessment is being prepared: it is not finished, and this page will say when it is.
Our products receive nothing through this website: the data they process is not covered by this page.

sections.title: Your rights
paragraphs: Under Québec's Law 25, the federal PIPEDA and, if you are in Europe, the GDPR, you may ask to access, correct or delete the information you sent us, withdraw your consent, and obtain a copy of it in a usual format. Write to us through the contact form and we will answer within 30 days.
If you are not satisfied, you may complain to the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada or, in Europe, to your data protection authority.

sections.title: Does a machine decide alone?
paragraphs: Under section 12.1 of the Act, a person must be told of a decision based exclusively on automated processing of their information at the latest when it is communicated to them. They may then ask which information was used and the reasons and main factors of the decision, have their information corrected, and submit their observations to a member of the team who can review the decision.

This website makes no decision about you based exclusively on automated processing. Its only automatic refusals protect the form against abuse: the bot check, the code sent to your address and the limit of five messages every ten minutes. They concern one sending, not you; if one of them blocks you, try again later or write to the person in charge named above.

Neither do our products in development. Verikora reads documents and flags what it sees, never scoring the person or giving a verdict on them: a person decides, Verikora decides nothing. Folioviv prepares tax returns; the merchant files them, and Folioviv transmits nothing to any government. Kridoc is in design and processes no information yet. Sovkora, the engine, returns its results to the product that calls it; it can automatically refuse a request whose content breaks its content policy, and that refusal concerns the request, not the person.

sections.title: If an incident affects your information
paragraphs: A confidentiality incident is an unauthorised access to, use or communication of personal information, or its loss. Under section 3.5 of the Act, when an incident presents a risk of serious injury, we must promptly notify the Commission d'accès à l'information and each person concerned. Under section 3.8, we must keep a register of these incidents and give it to the Commission on request.

The person in charge of the protection of personal information, the president of the company, assesses the risk and gives these notices. Our register is being set up, and this page will say when it is.
If you think an incident affects information you gave us, tell us through the contact form, at krizaka.com/contact (topic “Other”).

sections.title: Changes and contact
paragraphs: We update this page when what the website does changes, and the date at the top follows. For any privacy question, use the contact form (topic “Other”). Technologies Krizaka Inc., Montréal, Québec.

blocks.title: Six blocks. Each one deletes a bug you were about to write.
blocks.lead: Not a list of repositories: for each block, the trap most teams fall into, what the block does about it, what we refused and what it costs you. Every claim points to code or a test you can read.

forums.title: Questions go to two forums, not six.
forums.body: The five Java blocks ship as one BOM to one audience, and the useful questions cross them (users + billing + the service token): they share the Discussions of krizaka-platform-kit, one thread per block. Krizaka UI has its own — another ecosystem, another release cadence. Bugs stay on the repository they belong to.

page.feedbackBody: A block is right when it survives your code base, not ours. Ask in the block's thread, propose a change as an idea, or report a bug on its repository — every decision on this page is open to a better argument.
page.metaTitle: {name} — what it removes, what we chose and why

krizaka-platform-kit.name: Platform kit
krizaka-platform-kit.tagline: The cross-cutting code every Spring Boot service writes — written once, with its invariants tested.
krizaka-platform-kit.trap: Publishing an event right after the database write: on a crash between the two, the event is lost; send it first and a rollback has already told the world. A failing `@RabbitListener` requeued forever blocks its queue. Every service invents its own error JSON. Across Sovkora's services this code existed five to seven times — with three live bugs between the copies.
krizaka-platform-kit.answer: Four modules and four starters: one security baseline for every filter chain, events through a transactional outbox, consumer queues that retry then dead-letter, idempotent consumption, RFC 9457 errors with a request id, and required service names on every metric.
krizaka-platform-kit.rule: Nothing is open by omission. `SecurityBaseline` ends every chain with `anyRequest().authenticated()`: the path you forgot to list is closed, not public.
problem: Dual write: a service that writes its row then calls `rabbitTemplate.convertAndSend` loses the event when it crashes in between, and one that sends first announces changes that roll back.
Poison messages: a listener that throws on a malformed message is redelivered at once, forever, and nothing else in the queue moves.

Deduplication done by hand: a "does it exist? then insert" lets two overlapping deliveries both through — exactly when a broker redelivers a slow first attempt — and a claim kept after a failure silently drops the retry.
Security chains copied per service: two of six had drifted in Sovkora; one answered a CORS preflight with 401.

decisions.chose: A transactional outbox: `EventPublisher.publish` writes a row of your outbox in your transaction; a relay claims rows with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` and publishes them, with a `messageId` chosen at write time.
decisions.refused: Publishing to the broker from the service method, and a distributed transaction (XA) across database and broker.
decisions.because: The event commits or rolls back with the change. A relay that crashes republishes the same `messageId`, and the consumer's dedup makes it a no-op.
decisions.cost: An outbox table per context (you implement `OutboxStore` over your schema) and a polling delay between commit and publish.

decisions.chose: The envelope in AMQP headers (`kz-type`, `kz-version`, `kz-producer`, `kz-correlation-id`, `kz-occurred-at`), the body the bare event, and a JSON Schema per event in the producer's `-api` module.
decisions.refused: A shared jar of event DTOs, and a JSON wrapper around every body.
decisions.because: A shared DTO jar ties every service's release to every other's. A schema checked by tests on both sides (`EventContractTest`) gives the contract without the coupling, and the body stays readable by any language.
decisions.cost: Each consumer keeps its own tolerant copy of the event and one contract test.

decisions.chose: Quorum queues declared in one line (`KrizakaQueues.consumer`), a stateless retry with back-off — 5 attempts from 500 ms — then the queue’s `.dlq` twin with the original headers and the exception.
decisions.refused: Spring's default requeue on failure.
decisions.because: A requeued poison message loops forever; in the DLQ it is visible, with the reason, and can be replayed by hand.
decisions.cost: A queue already declared as classic must be drained and redeclared once.

decisions.chose: RFC 9457 Problem Details for every error: a `DomainException` becomes its 4xx with a stable code and the `requestId`; bean validation a 422 with `errors[]`; anything unexpected a 500 that never carries its message.
decisions.refused: Free-form error bodies per service, and stack traces or exception messages in 500 responses.
decisions.because: A client handles one shape, and the `requestId` in the response is the one in the log line — a support ticket points at the failure.
decisions.cost: Your exceptions extend `DomainException` (`NotFoundException`, `ConflictException`…) to choose their status.

decisions.chose: Starters that are POMs only, over modules usable alone; defaults applied at the lowest priority.
decisions.refused: Renaming the modules into starters, and defaults that override `application.yml`.
decisions.because: A product declares capabilities, not the Spring list behind them; a Spring Boot upgrade changes the starters, not your POM — and your `application.yml` always wins.
decisions.cost: Java 21 and Spring Boot 4.0 only.

notFor: Your services run on Spring Boot 3 or Java 17 — the kit targets Spring Boot 4.0 and Java 21.
Your HTTP layer is WebFlux: `krizaka-web` configures servlet applications only.
Your bus is Kafka: `krizaka-messaging` is RabbitMQ (AMQP 0-9-1) only.
Your tokens come from an external identity provider signing with RS256 or ES256: `krizaka-security` verifies HS256 today.
krizaka-platform-kit.status: 0.2.0 on Maven Central (2026-10-10): the four modules and the four starters, built and tested on real PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ in CI.

next.processOnce: `MessageDedup.processOnce` — claim, run, give the claim back on failure. Five listeners in notifications and billing repeat those eight lines today; one of them documents the forgotten release as "the settlement is lost forever". Lands in 0.3.0.
next.keys: One shared HS256 secret signs and verifies: a service that can verify can mint. Decided: issuer-signed session tokens (JWKS) and per-caller service tokens, HS256 deprecated over one minor.

krizaka-platform-kit.headline: An event published after the commit is lost on the next crash.
does: Events go through a transactional outbox: they commit or roll back with your data.
Queues retry 5 times, then dead-letter to `.dlq` — a poison message never loops.
One security baseline and RFC 9457 errors with a `requestId`, in every service.

krizaka-users.name: Users
krizaka-users.tagline: Sign-up, login, profiles, API keys and roles as a service — with a typed client for the others.
krizaka-users.trap: Sign-up looks like a weekend. Then come e-mail verification, reset tokens that must expire and be single-use, Google and GitHub accounts to link, API keys, roles in a JWT — and every other service validating that JWT its own way.
krizaka-users.answer: A Spring Boot service (or the `-core` you embed) that registers, verifies, logs in with a password or Google/GitHub, resets passwords, issues API keys and session JWTs carrying roles — and a client that every other service calls with a `SERVICE` token.
krizaka-users.rule: The owl keeps no secret in clear: a reset token is single-use, stored as a SHA-256 hash and dead after 15 minutes; a password is a BCrypt hash; a provider key is encrypted with AES-256 before it touches the disk.
problem: Reset links that work twice, never expire, or sit in the database in clear text — readable by anyone with a backup.
A users table that grows a column per product feature until another product cannot reuse it.
Every service calling the identity service on every request — identity down means everything down.

decisions.chose: Other services verify the session JWT locally (`krizaka-security`), with roles in the token.
decisions.refused: Calling the users service (token introspection) on every request.
decisions.because: The users service being down does not take the platform down, and a request costs no network hop.
decisions.cost: A revoked session stays valid until it expires (`PT12H` by default, `IDENTITY_JWT_TTL`).

decisions.chose: A profile is a theme plus attributes your application defines — the answers of an onboarding form whose JSON schema you supply — stored as given and never interpreted.
decisions.refused: A fixed profile model with product fields.
decisions.because: The service knows users, not your product; Sovkora's own fields moved out of it into its onboarding answers.
decisions.cost: Your code reads its attributes with its own defaults.

decisions.chose: A published contract (`krizaka-users-api`), a client with a per-entry cache, and an embeddable `-core`.
decisions.refused: A library that each application wires to its own tables.
decisions.because: One place hashes passwords and signs tokens; a fix lands once.
decisions.cost: A PostgreSQL database and RabbitMQ for its events (`evt.user.registered`, `evt.password.reset`).

notFor: You already run an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Entra ID): keep it.
You need SAML, enterprise SSO or multi-factor authentication: none of them is provided.
You need a revocation that takes effect before the token expires.
krizaka-users.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (api, client, core). 0.2.0 — event schemas checked against their producers — is merged and ships in November.

next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.
next.keys: Session tokens signed by this service only, verified with its JWKS by the others — no shared secret.

krizaka-users.headline: Sign-up looks like a weekend. Reset tokens, OAuth and JWTs make it a quarter.
does: Register, verify, log in with a password or Google/GitHub, reset — as a service.
Session JWTs carry the roles; every other service verifies them locally.
A typed `UserDirectoryClient` with a `SERVICE` token and a per-entry cache.

krizaka-notifications.name: Notifications
krizaka-notifications.tagline: E-mail, SMS and webhooks behind one event: applications never talk to an SMTP server again.
krizaka-notifications.trap: Each service that sends its own e-mails embeds an SMTP client, templates and retries. A provider outage becomes a bug in every one of them, and an e-mail sent inside a transaction that then rolls back cannot be unsent.
krizaka-notifications.answer: A service that consumes `evt.notification.requested` (and the users events), renders a template for the locale and delivers on the requested channel: SMTP, Twilio SMS, or an HTTP webhook.
krizaka-notifications.rule: The pigeon delivers each message once — or fails where you can see it. A channel that is not configured fails and goes to the dead-letter queue; it is never skipped in silence.
problem: A sign-up that fails because the mail server is slow.
A welcome e-mail for an account whose creation rolled back.
The same redelivered message sending the same e-mail twice.

decisions.chose: An event, published through the producer's outbox.
decisions.refused: A synchronous "send e-mail" HTTP endpoint.
decisions.because: No e-mail for a rolled-back change; an SMTP outage delays mail instead of failing sign-ups; a redelivery is sent once (deduplicated by `messageId`).
decisions.cost: RabbitMQ between your application and the service.

decisions.chose: Plain-text templates on disk, one file per template and locale, an en fallback, a directory you can point elsewhere without a rebuild.
decisions.refused: An HTML template engine, for now.
decisions.because: A template a non-developer can edit, and nothing to render that can break.
decisions.cost: Plain text only today.

decisions.chose: Webhooks only to hosts on an allow-list (empty = no webhooks).
decisions.refused: Any URL a requester sends.
decisions.because: An open webhook is a server-side request forgery waiting to happen.
decisions.cost: You declare the hosts.

notFor: You need open and click tracking, campaigns or rich HTML e-mails: use a marketing e-mail service.
Your application has no message broker and won't run one.
You need mobile push: not a channel yet.
krizaka-notifications.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (the `-api` contract). The service is built from source or as an image; 0.2.0 ships in November.

next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.

krizaka-notifications.headline: An e-mail sent inside a transaction that rolls back can't be unsent.
does: Publish `evt.notification.requested` in your transaction — no SMTP client in your service.
Plain-text templates per locale, `en` as the fallback.
E-mail (SMTP), SMS (Twilio) or a webhook to allow-listed hosts: the same request.

krizaka-billing.name: Billing & credits
krizaka-billing.tagline: Credits, wallets, plans, a versioned price book and metering: hold → settle → release.
krizaka-billing.trap: Charging for expensive work goes wrong two ways: debit afterwards and the work ran on credit nobody had; debit up front and a failed job is billed. Then a "job done" message is redelivered and the same job is debited twice.
krizaka-billing.answer: A service and a typed client: a caller holds the estimated credits before expensive work, then settles the measured cost or releases the hold. Holds that are never settled expire. Plans, subscriptions, packs, wallets and usage analytics around it.
krizaka-billing.rule: The flamingo gets paid for what was done, once — and nobody pays for work that failed. A failed job releases its hold; every debit carries an idempotency key.
problem: A user who starts ten expensive jobs at once with credit for one.
A failed render billed at its estimate.

decisions.chose: Hold → settle → release, with an expiry on holds.
decisions.refused: Debit after the work, and prepay without reservation.
decisions.because: Work never starts without the credit to cover it, and failure costs nothing.
decisions.cost: One synchronous call (hold) on the request path; settle and release are off it.

decisions.chose: An append-only ledger where every debit carries an idempotency key, on top of message deduplication.
decisions.refused: Trusting deduplication alone.
decisions.because: Two independent guards: a redelivery that gets past one still debits once.
decisions.cost: The ledger only grows; corrections are new entries.

decisions.chose: Prices and the hold lifetime are rows of a versioned price book; a hold pins the version it was priced at.
decisions.refused: Prices in code or configuration.
decisions.because: Repricing never changes what an in-flight job costs, and needs no deployment.
decisions.cost: A price change is a data migration you review.

decisions.chose: A no-op adapter when `krizaka.billing.enabled` is false.
decisions.refused: `if (billingEnabled)` at every call site.
decisions.because: The same code runs metered and unmetered.
decisions.cost: None worth naming.

notFor: You need invoices, taxes or card payments: billing counts credits; collecting money is yours (a top-up credits a wallet).
Your capabilities are not AI work — today. The contract still names Sovkora's (CHAT, IMAGE, AUDIO, VIDEO, AGENT) and its measurements (tokens, GPU seconds…); see below.
krizaka-billing.status: 0.1.0 on Maven Central (api, client). 0.2.0 — the outbox implements `OutboxStore.append`, every event has its JSON Schema — is merged and ships in November.

next.vocabulary: Decided: capabilities and units become keys declared in the price book, measurements a map of quantities; Sovkora keeps its enums in Sovkora. A reusable billing block cannot speak one product's vocabulary.
next.release: BOM 0.2.0 manages this block at an unpublished 0.2.0: declare 0.1.0 explicitly until BOM 0.3.0.

krizaka-billing.headline: Debit after and the work ran on credit nobody had. Debit before and failures get billed.
does: `hold` the estimate before the work, then `settleMeasured` or `release`.
Every debit carries an idempotency key: a redelivered message is charged once.
Plans, subscriptions, packs and wallets around an append-only ledger.

krizaka-build.name: Build, BOM & test kit
krizaka-build.tagline: The parent POM, the BOM and the governance tests behind every com.krizaka artifact.
krizaka-build.trap: Every multi-repository Java organisation ends up with parent POMs that drift: a module on another Java, unpinned plugins, a POM that Maven Central rejects for a missing licence block. And a BOM that imports Spring's silently overrides the Spring Boot version you chose.
krizaka-build.answer: `krizaka-parent` (Central metadata, Java 21, formatting checked, unit and integration tests, coverage, a signed release in one command), `krizaka-bom` (the compatible set of every com.krizaka artifact) and `krizaka-test-support` (architecture rules, one PostgreSQL + RabbitMQ per test run, event contract tests).
krizaka-build.rule: A rule that judges nothing passes nothing. Every rule of the test kit fails on an empty population — a typo in a package name cannot turn a check into a green tick.
problem: Conventions in a wiki: true on the day they are written.
One Testcontainers setup per repository, each starting its own database per test class.
A minor release that breaks binary compatibility, discovered by the people who upgraded.

decisions.chose: A BOM that carries only com.krizaka artifacts; the parent has no `dependencyManagement` of its own.
decisions.refused: Importing `spring-boot-dependencies` in our BOM.
decisions.because: Importing `krizaka-bom` must never pin a version you chose. Your Spring Boot BOM stays yours; ours sits beside it.
decisions.cost: You import Spring Boot's BOM (or parent) yourself.

decisions.chose: Architecture rules as tests (`CodeRules`, `SourceRules`, `ConfigBindingRules`: layering, constructor injection, private state, no Environment injection…).
decisions.refused: A review checklist.
decisions.because: A rule that runs on every build is the only kind still true six months later.
decisions.cost: Rules are opinionated: take the ones that fit, call them from your own test.

decisions.chose: japicmp in the release profile: a binary break in a minor fails the release; publication on Central confirmed by hand.
decisions.refused: SemVer by good intentions, and automatic publication.
decisions.because: A release on Central can never be deleted: a break shipped is a break forever.
decisions.cost: A deliberate break is declared in the repository for that release.

notFor: You do not publish to Maven Central and don't want our conventions (google-java-format, Java 21) on your build: import the BOM, skip the parent.
You are on Java 17 or earlier.

next.bom: BOM 0.2.0 names users, notifications and billing at a 0.2.0 that is not published yet. Decided: a BOM release resolves every artifact it manages before it is signed; BOM 0.3.0 waits for the three.

krizaka-build.headline: Parent POMs drift — and a Spring BOM silently overrides the Boot version you chose.
does: `krizaka-parent`: Java 21, pinned plugins, Central metadata, a signed release in one command.
`krizaka-bom`: the compatible set of every `com.krizaka` artifact, and nothing else.
`krizaka-test-support`: architecture rules, real PostgreSQL + RabbitMQ, event contract tests.

krizaka-ui.name: Krizaka UI
krizaka-ui.tagline: Tokens, a Tailwind v4 preset, accessible primitives, icons and i18n — web and React Native.
krizaka-ui.trap: Three products, three token vocabularies: we measured 1,153 `light:` overrides in one application, the same card written five times, and focus traps, keyboard handling and ARIA rewritten by hand in each kit.
krizaka-ui.answer: One semantic vocabulary (`--kz-*`) compiled from design tokens, a preset that turns it into Tailwind utilities, and primitives — button, card, dialog, field, tabs, toast, command palette… — with React Native parity, one entry point each. The documentation of every component is generated from its code.
krizaka-ui.rule: The owl reads the code, not a wiki: every component's page on ui.krizaka.com is generated from its `meta.ts` and its named examples, and the registry tests fail when one is missing.
problem: A theme implemented as `light:` and dark: variants in every component — a new theme means touching all of them.
Accessibility rewritten per product, and wrong in at least one.
A documentation site that describes last quarter's props.

decisions.chose: One token vocabulary; dark on `:root`, light on `html.light`; a brand overrides values (`brands/scoped.css`).
decisions.refused: `light:/dark:` variants in components, and a token set per product.
decisions.because: A theme or a brand is a set of values: Sovkora’s orange and Folioviv’s green use the same components as this site.
decisions.cost: Components read `var(--kz-*)` only; raw palette colours are refused by the lint rules.

decisions.chose: Radix for every non-trivial interaction, variants with tailwind-variants, every story audited by axe in dark and light on each pull request.
decisions.refused: Hand-written focus traps and keyboard handling.
decisions.because: Accessibility is written once and tested where it is written.
decisions.cost: Radix in your bundle; size-limit budgets per entry keep it in check.

decisions.chose: Words arrive as props; no translation function inside the library.
decisions.refused: Bundling a translation runtime.
decisions.because: Any i18n works — ours (`@krizaka/i18n`, typed catalogues and a CI check) or yours.
decisions.cost: You pass the labels.

decisions.chose: A ratchet: per-repository counters of raw palette classes, `light:` variants, `[var(--…)]` utilities and className templates that may only go down.
decisions.refused: A big-bang migration, and a lint rule switched on at once.
decisions.because: An existing application adopts it screen by screen without letting the debt grow back.
decisions.cost: A `lint-ratchet.json` to commit and a check in CI.

notFor: You don't use Tailwind v4: the preset requires it (the tokens alone are plain CSS variables).
You want an unstyled kit and own every pixel: use Radix directly.
You need charts today: `@krizaka/charts` is being built.
krizaka-ui.status: @krizaka/ui, tokens and tailwind 2.2.0 on npm (latest) — 2.2.0 brought the five birds of this page (`@krizaka/ui/mascots`); icons, i18n, intl and config 0.1.0. Supported: majors N and N-1, fixes for six months after N+1.

next.charts: `@krizaka/charts` — theme- and brand-aware charts on Apache ECharts, each with an accessible data table, and the effects and blocks after it: the roadmap is an open epic.

krizaka-ui.headline: Three products, three token vocabularies, 1,153 `light:` overrides in one app.
does: One semantic vocabulary, `--kz-*`, compiled from design tokens — dark and light alike.
Accessible primitives with React Native parity, one entry point each.
Every component's documentation generated from its code.
